pos: n. (the second son of David, borne by Abigail at Hebron; called Daniel in 1 Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Kil'ab, probably like his father, or restraint of the father; the Authorized Version margin at 2 Samuel 3:3 gives “or, Daniel,” the name under which 1 Chronicles 3:1 records him.
biblical_def: Chileab was David's second son, born at Hebron: “And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur” (2 Samuel 3:3). The Chronicler gives the same man another name: “Now these were the sons of David, which were born unto him in Hebron; the firstborn Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; the second Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess” (1 Chronicles 3:1), and the Authorized Version margin at 2 Samuel notes the equivalence. He is not Daniel the prophet; he is David's son by the woman who had been Nabal's wife. Nothing else is recorded of him — no exploit, no sin, no death — and that silence is itself worth something. His elder brother Amnon raped his sister; his younger brother Absalom murdered Amnon and then rebelled against his father. Chileab is the one son of Hebron who never appears again. The house was born in a season of attrition: “Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1), and the sons listed in those verses — by several different mothers — are the fruit of a polygamy that would tear the household apart.

corruption_summary: David's many wives are read as a cultural detail, where 2 Samuel lists the sons of several mothers and then narrates the household destroying itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The list of sons born at Hebron is a list of different mothers, and the chapters that follow are rape, fratricide and rebellion inside that one household. Scripture does not editorialise; it narrates, and the narration is the judgment. The dictionary holds marriage as one man and one woman, which is the creational ordinance the Lord Himself appeals to, and it reads the collapse of David's family as the Bible's own commentary on departing from it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a son of whom nothing bad is recorded is a mercy in a chapter of disasters, and that one man may be given two names in Scripture without the record being in error.

pos: n. (a place or sanctuary in Moab named in Isaiah's burden against that nation; named once)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Bayith, the house, from bayith, a house; it may be the proper name of a Moabite shrine or simply the temple of Moab's god. Named once in Scripture, at Isaiah 15:2.
biblical_def: Bajith is named once, in Isaiah's burden against Moab: “He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off” (Isaiah 15:2). The Hebrew is simply the house, and interpreters have taken it either as the proper name of a place or as the temple of Chemosh — the house, as a Moabite would say it. Either way the picture is of a stricken nation going up to its sanctuary to weep. The oracle opens in the dark: “The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence” (Isaiah 15:1), and the refugees run south: “his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old” (Isaiah 15:5). What makes this prophecy remarkable is Isaiah's own grief — My heart shall cry out for Moab — and the verdict on the praying: “And it shall come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary on the high place, that he shall come to his sanctuary to pray; but he shall not prevail” (Isaiah 16:12).

corruption_summary: Sincere prayer is assumed to be effective prayer, where Isaiah says Moab will go to its sanctuary and pray and shall not prevail.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 16:12 is one of the most uncomfortable verses in the prophets for a pluralist age: Moab prays, wearily and in earnest, and does not prevail. The sincerity is not questioned and the outcome is not in doubt. Prayer is not a human technique that works on whatever god it is aimed at; it is access granted through a Mediator, and there is one. The dictionary holds this and also holds Isaiah's own tears over Moab, which are in the same oracle.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a prophet may weep for the people he is sent to condemn, and that grief over the lost is not softness about their condition.

pos: n. (a chief of the Levites who gave liberally for Josiah's passover; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Konanyahu, the LORD has established, from kun, to establish, with the divine name; named once in Scripture, at 2 Chronicles 35:9.
biblical_def: Conaniah is named once, among the Levites who furnished the greatest passover in Israel's history out of their own property: “Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethaneel, his brethren, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, chief of the Levites, gave unto the Levites for passover offerings five thousand small cattle, and five hundred oxen” (2 Chronicles 35:9). His name means the LORD has established. The occasion is Josiah's reformation at its height: “Moreover Josiah kept a passover unto the LORD in Jerusalem: and they killed the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month” (2 Chronicles 35:1). The giving ran downward from the top: the king gave from his substance, then “his princes gave willingly unto the people, to the priests, and to the Levites: Hilkiah and Zechariah and Jehiel, rulers of the house of God, gave unto the priests for the passover offerings two thousand and six hundred small cattle, and three hundred oxen” (2 Chronicles 35:8), and then Conaniah and his brethren gave to the Levites. Nobody was taxed; the leaders paid. And the verdict stands in the same chapter: “And there was no passover like to that kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet” (2 Chronicles 35:18).

corruption_summary: Reformation is imagined as a matter of preaching alone, where Josiah's passover was paid for out of the pockets of the king, the princes and the Levitical chiefs.
corruption_paragraphs: The greatest passover since Samuel was funded by the men who led it. The king gave from his own substance, the princes gave willingly, and the Levitical chiefs gave to their own brethren, and the chapter counts the animals. A reformation that costs its leaders nothing is unlikely to be one. The pattern here is not a levy on the people but generosity flowing downward from those with most to give.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that recovered worship is expensive and that the men whose names Scripture keeps are the ones who paid for it.

pos: n. (the grandfather of Jaazaniah, head of the house of the Rechabites; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chabatsinyah, of uncertain meaning; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 35:3.
biblical_def: Habaziniah is named once, in the pedigree of the man Jeremiah brought into the temple to shame Judah: “Then I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habaziniah, and his brethren, and all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites” (Jeremiah 35:3). The prophet set wine before them and told them to drink, and they refused: “But they said, We will drink no wine: for Jonadab the son of Rechab our father commanded us, saying, Ye shall drink no wine, neither ye, nor your sons for ever” (Jeremiah 35:6). The whole episode was staged for a comparison, and the LORD made it explicit: “The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab, that he commanded his sons not to drink wine, are performed; for unto this day they drink none, but obey their father's commandment: notwithstanding I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye hearkened not unto me” (Jeremiah 35:14). A family kept a merely human father's word for two centuries; Judah would not keep God's. And the Rechabites got a promise for it: “Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever” (Jeremiah 35:19).

corruption_summary: The Rechabites' abstinence is taken as a command to the church, when Jeremiah 35 commends their obedience to a father and says nothing to bind anyone else's cup.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 35 is a favourite text of the teetotal argument, and it will not carry it. God commends the Rechabites for keeping Jonadab's charge, not for the content of the charge; the point of comparison is obedience, and the rebuke falls on Judah for disobeying God, not on Judah for drinking wine. Scripture gives wine as a blessing and condemns drunkenness as a sin, and a dictionary that honours the text will not turn a commendation of filial faithfulness into a dietary law.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a family's two-century obedience to a father's word was used by God to indict a nation's contempt for His own, and that such faithfulness carries a promise.

pos: n. (a son of Zerubbabel in the royal line after the captivity; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chashubah, consideration or esteemed, from chashab, to think or reckon; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 3:20.
biblical_def: Hashubah is named once, in the line of David after the exile: “And Hashubah, and Ohel, and Berechiah, and Hasadiah, Jushabhesed, five” (1 Chronicles 3:20). His name means esteemed, or consideration, from the verb to reckon. The register is one of the most important short passages in the Old Testament, because it carries the house of David through the captivity: “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17) — Jeconiah being the king of whom Jeremiah said that no son of his would sit upon the throne — and then “And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:19). Hashubah and his four brothers follow, and the line continues: “And the sons of Hananiah; Pelatiah, and Jesaiah: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shechaniah” (1 Chronicles 3:21). Zerubbabel was the governor through whom the second temple was built, and the Lord called him His signet. His obscure sons are the link between the ruined throne and the Christ who would occupy it.

corruption_summary: The Davidic line is spoken of as having failed at the captivity, when Chronicles traces it straight through Jeconiah and Zerubbabel to the obscure sons who carried it on.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah pronounced that no son of Jeconiah would sit on David's throne, and the throne did stand empty. But the line did not end, and 1 Chronicles 3 records it continuing through men nobody has heard of — Hashubah, Ohel, Hasadiah, Jushabhesed — until it arrives, in Matthew's hands, at Christ. The promise to David was never carried by the office alone; it was carried by a family God kept.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God preserved the house of David through a captivity and five obscure brothers, and that a man named esteemed was esteemed by the only reckoning that counts.

pos: n. (a name borne by two captains: a Manassite who defected to David, and the chief of Judah's thousands under Jehoshaphat)
etymology: Hebrew 'Adnach and 'Adnah, probably pleasure or rest, from a root meaning to be delicate or luxurious; borne by two men in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Adnah is borne by two captains. The first came over to David at Ziklag while Saul still reigned: “As he went to Ziklag, there fell to him of Manasseh, Adnah, and Jozabad, and Jediael, and Michael, and Jozabad, and Elihu, and Zilthai, captains of the thousands that were of Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 12:20). The Chronicler describes the whole movement in a line worth memorising: “For at that time day by day there came to David to help him, until it was a great host, like the host of God” (1 Chronicles 12:22), and the chapter ends in national unity: “All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel: and all the rest also of Israel were of one heart to make David king” (1 Chronicles 12:38). The second Adnah served two centuries later as the chief captain of Judah: “And these are the numbers of them according to the house of their fathers: Of Judah, the captains of thousands; Adnah the chief, and with him mighty men of valour three hundred thousand” (2 Chronicles 17:14). The dictionary records the distinction so that the Manassite defector is not merged with Jehoshaphat's general.

corruption_summary: Defection from a failing authority to a rightful one is read as mere opportunism, where Chronicles calls it coming with a perfect heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The men who left Saul for David were deserting a king God had rejected for a king God had anointed, and the Chronicler does not call it treachery. He calls it coming with a perfect heart to make David king. Judging such a movement requires knowing which authority is the lawful one, and Scripture is willing to say. Loyalty is owed to the rightful claim, not to the present occupant as such.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God built David's host day by day until it was like the host of God, and that two men may bear one name across two centuries without being confused.

pos: n. (the father of Shaphan the scribe, who carried the book of the law to Josiah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Atsalyahu, the LORD has reserved or set apart, from a root meaning to reserve, with the divine name; named twice in Scripture, at 2 Kings 22:3 and 2 Chronicles 34:8.
biblical_def: Azaliah is named twice, both times as the father of the man who carried the recovered book of the law to the king: “And it came to pass in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, that the king sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, the son of Meshullam, the scribe, to the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 22:3). The Chronicler gives the same errand: “Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had purged the land, and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, and Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God” (2 Chronicles 34:8). His name means the LORD has reserved, and what his son was reserved for was one of the great hinges of Old Testament history. The errand was ordinary building repair; what came of it was not: “And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it” (2 Kings 22:8). Shaphan read it to Josiah, “And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes” (2 Kings 22:11). A nation's reformation began with a workman's errand and a scribe who read aloud.

corruption_summary: Reformation is expected to begin with a programme, where Josiah's began with a repair crew, a found book, and a king who tore his clothes.
corruption_paragraphs: The sequence in 2 Kings 22 is worth attending to. There was no strategy. A king sent his scribe to pay builders, the high priest handed over a book that had been lost in the house of God, the scribe read it, and the king rent his clothes. Every real reformation in the church has had that shape: the word recovered, read plainly, and received with grief before it is received with joy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Scriptures do their own work when they are simply read aloud, and that a man named the LORD has reserved fathered the reader.

pos: n. (one of the leaders who came up from Babylon with Zerubbabel; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew Bilshan, of uncertain meaning, perhaps searcher or inquirer; named at Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7.
biblical_def: Bilshan is one of the eleven or twelve men named at the head of the great return from Babylon. Ezra lists them: “Which came with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, Baanah” (Ezra 2:2). Nehemiah gives the same company with some names in their alternate forms: “Who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah” (Nehemiah 7:7). Bilshan's name is spelled the same in both, and the two lists together are a small lesson in how Scripture records a thing twice without contradiction: some men are given by two names, and the Authorized Version margins note the equivalences. The returning company is described in the verse before: “Now these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity, of those which had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away unto Babylon, and came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1). And what the whole roll was for appears a chapter later: “And when the seventh month was come, and the children of Israel were in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem” (Ezra 3:1). The point of being counted was to be gathered.

corruption_summary: Parallel lists with differing names are treated as contradictions, where the Authorized Version's own margins note that several men went by two names.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7 list the same company with four names differing, and the critical conclusion is corruption or confusion of sources. The Authorized Version translators, working from the Hebrew, simply noted in the margin that Seraiah is also called Azariah. Men in that world often bore two names, as Simon was Peter and Saul was Paul. The dictionary does not grant that a double name is a defect in the record.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the point of being numbered in Ezra's roll was to be gathered as one man to Jerusalem, and that a careful reader of two lists finds harmony where a hasty one finds error.

pos: n. (the father of Ahi, chief of a house of the tribe of Gad; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Abdi'el, servant of God, from 'ebed, a servant, and 'El, God; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 5:15.
biblical_def: Abdiel is named once, in the register of the tribes east of Jordan: “Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 5:15). His name means servant of God. The households he belonged to held some of the best grazing land in Israel: “And they dwelt in Gilead in Bashan, and in her towns, and in all the suburbs of Sharon, upon their borders” (1 Chronicles 5:16). The chapter then gives one of the most striking statements in Chronicles about a battle. First the muster: “The sons of Reuben, and the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war, were four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore, that went out to the war” (1 Chronicles 5:18). Then the verdict on the result: “For there fell down many slain, because the war was of God. And they dwelt in their steads until the captivity” (1 Chronicles 5:22). The war was of God — that is the Chronicler's explanation of the casualties and of the conquest together. And the last clause is the shadow over the whole chapter: these eastern tribes held their land until the captivity, and then lost it first.

corruption_summary: Military outcomes are explained by force of arms alone, where Chronicles says flatly that the war was of God and accounts for the dead on that ground.
corruption_paragraphs: “There fell down many slain, because the war was of God” is a sentence no secular military history can write. It attributes both the victory and the casualties to God's purpose, in one clause, without apology. The dictionary takes it as it stands: God governs battles, including the dying in them, and the forty-four thousand skilful bowmen of the eastern tribes were instruments and not causes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the tribes who settled east of Jordan dwelt in their steads until the captivity and then lost them first, and that the Chronicler notes it without sentiment.

pos: n. (the third son of Benjamin in the Chronicles register; also spelled Ahiram and Aher elsewhere)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achrach, probably after the brother, or brother's follower; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 8:1, and generally identified with the Ahiram of Numbers 26:38.
biblical_def: Aharah is named once, as Benjamin's third son in the Chronicler's register of the tribe: “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1), and the list completes itself in the next verse: “Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth” (1 Chronicles 8:2). The same man appears in the wilderness census as Ahiram, and in another Chronicles list as Aher; the Authorized Version keeps each spelling where it found it, and the dictionary names the equivalence here so that three spellings are not taken for three men. The chapter goes on through the Benjamite households and their resettlements: “And these are the sons of Ehud: these are the heads of the fathers of the inhabitants of Geba, and they removed them to Manahath” (1 Chronicles 8:6). And it closes with the reason the whole register exists: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Benjamin was the tribe that stayed with Judah when the kingdom split, the tribe of Saul and of Paul, and almost destroyed in the days of the judges. Its register is a record of survival.

corruption_summary: Variant spellings of one name across parallel registers are read as evidence of unreliable transmission rather than as the ordinary condition of ancient Hebrew records.
corruption_paragraphs: Aharah, Ahiram and Aher are one man under three spellings, and the Authorized Version preserves each as it stood. The critical habit treats such variation as proof that the lists are late compilations from confused sources. The believing position is simpler and more probable: Hebrew names took several written forms, the inspired writers recorded what their sources gave them, and the identity of the man is recoverable by anyone who compares the lists.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Benjamin, nearly destroyed in the days of the judges, is registered here as heads of the fathers and chief men dwelling in Jerusalem.
